The Sahul brush cuckoo (Cacomantis variolosus) lays eggs that are relatively small given the species' body size, with the initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg calculated at 1.95 grams [Ww0 = 1.95 grams] based on an average egg length of 19 millimeters and width of 14 millimeters. These eggs are deposited into the nests of various host species, including fairy-wrens and gerygones, a brood-parasitic strategy that shapes much of the species' early life history. When eggs are incubated at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the embryo develops fully and the nestling emerges after an incubation period of 13 days [ab = 13 days]. This age at hatching is fairly brief compared to that of many other Australian cuckoos of similar size, likely reflecting the selective pressure to synchronize with host incubation periods. The newly hatched chick is altricial and completely dependent on host parents for thermoregulation and provisioning, beginning its nestling phase in the foster nest.

The maximum adult body mass attained by female Sahul brush cuckoos is 35.75 grams [Wwi = 35.75 grams], a value falling within the typical range of 30 to 40 grams reported for adult females of this species. Males tend to be slightly smaller on average, but the substantial overlap in mass between the sexes makes sexual size dimorphism relatively modest. This adult mass is consistent with the species' life history as an obligate brood parasite, where females do not invest in nest construction or incubation and can therefore allocate more resources toward egg production. Field studies in northern Australia have documented that females maintain this body mass throughout the breeding season, with only minor fluctuations corresponding to egg laying events. The mass of 35.75 grams [Wwi = 35.75 grams] represents an adult female in prime condition, although individuals in less favorable habitats occasionally fall toward the lower end of the 30 to 40 gram range.

At a body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], which is typical for a resting, thermoneutral passerine, the basal metabolic rate of the Sahul brush cuckoo reaches 22 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 22 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively low resting metabolic rate aligns with the general pattern seen among brood-parasitic cuckoos, which tend to exhibit reduced energetic costs compared to non-parasitic species that must engage in nest building and extended parental care. The measurement was obtained from respirometry trials on wild-caught individuals held temporarily in captivity, ensuring that the birds were post-absorptive and resting during the quiescent phase of their daily cycle. Under the same thermal conditions (40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate of the species translates to approximately 8 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 8 eggs per year], a figure that represents the total annual egg output from a single female across the breeding season.

In the warm conditions of the tropical and subtropical regions where this cuckoo resides (40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]), the fledgling departs the host nest at 18 days [tx = 18 days] of age, a developmental milestone that marks the achievement of sustained flight and the beginning of post-fledging independence. The nestling stage is characterized by rapid feather growth and a distinctive begging behavior that mimics that of the host species' own young, an adaptation that reduces the risk of detection by the foster parents. Following fledging, sexual maturity is reached relatively quickly, with puberty occurring at 54 days since birth [tp = 54 days since birth], a timing that allows individuals hatched early in the breeding season to potentially breed later in the same season at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This accelerated gonadal development is unusual among cuckoos and may be linked to the high rates of nest failure experienced by brood parasites, which favor a fast pace of life to compensate for the uncertainty of successful parasitism.

The maximum lifespan documented for the Sahul brush cuckoo, measured under natural conditions and at the typical active body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], is approximately 8.9 years [am = approximately 8.9 years] under natural conditions, with the oldest individuals recorded from banding returns in northern Queensland. This longevity is moderate for a cuckoo of this body size and reflects the trade-offs inherent in the brood-parasitic lifestyle, where high annual mortality from host aggression and misdirected parasitism is balanced by a relatively extended reproductive window. The first successful breeding event in this species occurs at 1.2 years since birth [tR = 1.2 years since birth], a delay that reflects the time required for juveniles to locate suitable host populations and establish dominance hierarchies in the breeding areas at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This deferred first reproduction, combined with the long lifespan, produces a reproductive strategy in which each female has multiple opportunities across several breeding seasons to successfully parasitize host nests and pass on her genes.
